approachQuestion.prompt: A browser starts at home. Process at most 200,000 commands VISIT(url), BACK, FORWARD. URLs are immutable IDs from a fixed-size domain. BACK/FORWARD at an end are no-ops. VISIT after BACK discards the forward branch. Return the current URL ID after every command. Example VISIT(a), VISIT(b), BACK, VISIT(c), FORWARD -> [a,b,a,c,c].

options.text: Maintain current URL and back/forward stacks. On VISIT, push current onto back, set current to the new URL, and clear forward. BACK/ FORWARD move current between the stacks.
options.feedback: A new visit preserves the page just left as a back destination and invalidates only the abandoned forward branch.

options.text: Keep all pages in an array and an index. BACK/FORWARD move the index; VISIT truncates the suffix after the index and appends the new URL.
options.feedback: This is also optimal: each page entry is appended once and removed at most once over the command sequence, while index movement is constant time.

options.text: Use one stack and pop on BACK, discarding the page just left.
options.feedback: Without saving the departed page, BACK loses the page needed by FORWARD.

options.text: On VISIT clear both history stacks and set current to the new URL.
options.feedback: This destroys valid back history: after VISIT(a), VISIT(b), BACK must restore a.

feedback.reason: The new visit c clears the old forward page b, so final FORWARD leaves c current.
details: Maintain current URL and back/forward stacks. On VISIT, push current onto back, set current to the new URL, and clear forward. BACK/ FORWARD move current between the stacks.

A new VISIT after BACK creates a new branch and clears forward history. Otherwise FORWARD could incorrectly return to the abandoned branch. Clearing many entries costs time, but each cleared entry was previously added.

“Maintain current URL and back/forward stacks. On VISIT, push current onto back, set current to the new URL, and clear forward. BACK/ FORWARD move current between the stacks.”: A new visit preserves the page just left as a back destination and invalidates only the abandoned forward branch.

“Keep all pages in an array and an index. BACK/FORWARD move the index; VISIT truncates the suffix after the index and appends the new URL.”: This is also optimal: each page entry is appended once and removed at most once over the command sequence, while index movement is constant time.
“Use one stack and pop on BACK, discarding the page just left.”: Without saving the departed page, BACK loses the page needed by FORWARD.
“On VISIT clear both history stacks and set current to the new URL.”: This destroys valid back history: after VISIT(a), VISIT(b), BACK must restore a.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For browser-back-forward-history-optimal, let n be the number of input operations or tokens. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: The input is immutable; returned output is excluded from auxiliary space. All stack operations and value comparisons take constant time.
The algorithm is iterative with O(1) call-stack use. The auxiliary stack may hold up to n fixed-size entries.
No hashing, recursion, or hidden array copy occurs. Any movement between stacks counts as constant time per item.

options.text: O(log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: History movement and clearing have linear total work over the command sequence.
details: The new visit c clears the old forward page b, so final FORWARD leaves c current. Each item is processed a bounded number of times and the working stack can retain a linear number of entries.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A sequence of VISIT commands leaves a linear number of pages in back history even without any FORWARD output.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: A history entry cleared by VISIT was previously created or moved there; all such clears are charged to earlier commands, not repeated full replays.
“O(log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The last navigation command can change the reported current page, so worst-case processing reads every command.
